newsitem.title: KENYA: FEATURE - Flying Kenyan flowers costs less as volume rises.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Flying Kenyan flowers costs less as volume rises.

text.p: The cost of airfreighting flowers, fruit and vegetables from Kenya has dropped as more carriers offer flights in response to booming horticultural production.
The Kenyan capital, Nairobi, is widely regarded as the air-hub of East Africa and the bulk of air cargo comes from exports of fresh produce. About 90 percent of all horticultural exports are by air.

Flowers make up the biggest share of Kenya's total horticulture exports with close to 40,000 tonnes of total exports. Fruit and vegetables account for 35,000 and 10,000 tonnes respectively, according to statistics issued by the Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya (FPEAK).

"All flowers, most vegetables and a fairly high percentage of fruits are shipped out by air," said Dr David Grey, an expert in horticulture associated with British consultants Pathfast Publishing, a group specialising in floriculture trade.
"Although many of the smaller exporting countries are concerned about the lack of airspace, it seems that as production increases so does the number of would-be carriers.
"In Kenya the freight rate has dropped over the past

three years from $2.15 per kg (2.2lb) to $1.70 per kg," Grey told a seminar at Kenya's annual horticulture exhibition, the three-day Hortec '97, which is the biggest exhibition of its type in sub-Saharan Africa.
"In volume terms fresh horticulture exports recorded 57,364 metric tonnes in 1992, rising to 71,758 tonnes in 1995," FPEAK chairman Simon Ethangatta said.
"1996 has done even better with a record high of 84,824 tonnes, a 18.2 percent increase in volume over 1995 exports," he added.
Horticulture exports in 1995 were worth $193 million in foreign exchange earnings, but 1996 figures were not available.
FLOWER EXPORTS BLOOMING
Ethangatta said the latest figures from flower auctions in the Netherlands showed a clear increase in exports to markets in Russia and East Europe, and new markets were springing up globally.
Grey said that in recent years exports of cut flowers to the European market had been dominated by production from developing countries.

"Our statistics still largely ignore another increasingly important area for our trade, Russia and Eastern Europe. Neither should the Far East markets such as Taiwan, China and Korea be ignored...particularly in cut flowers and foliage.

"Most of the future expansions in the interantional trade will come from newer consuming countries as they open up their borders. For instance, Russia and Eastern Europe are beginning to import appreciable numbers of flowers and plants," Grey said.
He said that, while imports of cut flowers to Europe had almost doubled in the last 12 years, exports from Africa to Europe had increased eight-fold.
International trade in cut flowers in 1996 increased to $3.15 billion worth of sales, up from $2.71 billion in 1995, a growth of 16 percent, Grey said.
He added that in recent years exports of cut flowers to the European market had been dominated by production from developing countries
"The most dramatic change in the last few years has been the emergence of Africa, particularly East and Central Africa, as the major supplier area to the European market.

"There has been a realisation in many of the developing countries as to the potential benefits of the floriculture trade to their economies. Developed countries such as Israel, Colombia and Morocco are finding that they are losing market share, especially to countries with lower production costs such as Kenya, Zimbabwe, Costa Rica and Ecuador," Grey concluded.
About 32 percent of Kenya's horticulture exports goes to the Netherlands, some 28 percent to Britain and much of the rest to other European countries.
